stops.name: Cameliard, the court of Leodegrance
stops.campa: In the western march called Cameliard, King Leodegrance keeps a court whose chief treasure is not gold, and in it a daughter grows whose beauty later chroniclers will not tire of praising. Since Uther Pendragon's day the king has guarded a great round board of oak, a hundred and fifty places cut for as many knights, waiting for the hand that will complete its fellowship. Guinevere is raised among its empty seats, taught the courtesies of a hall built for equals, not knowing that her own marriage will carry the Table out of her father's keeping and into the world's memory.

stops.name: The wedding at Camelot, and the gift of the Round Table
stops.campa: Merlin comes to Cameliard for Arthur and asks Leodegrance for his daughter. The old king answers that it is the best tidings he ever heard, and that he will send with her a gift dearer than land: the Round Table Uther once gave him, complete at a hundred and fifty sieges, and a hundred knights of his own, for fifty have been slain in his days. Guinevere rides out with Merlin, by water and by land in great royalty, until they come nigh unto London, and she is wedded to Arthur at Camelot in the church of Saint Stephen's, the Table set up behind her, its empty chairs still waiting.
stops.quote: I shall give him the Table Round, the which Uther Pendragon gave me, and when it is full complete, there is an hundred knights and fifty.
stops.quote_source: Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book III, ch. 1

stops.name: Camelot, the fellowship sworn
stops.campa: At the high feast of Pentecost the young knights kneel around the Table and swear the oath Arthur sets them: to do no outrage and no murder, to flee treason, to give mercy to whoever asks it, to succour ladies, damosels and gentlewomen upon pain of death, and never to take up battle in a wrongful quarrel. Guinevere sits crowned beside her husband as the vow is renewed year on year, the hall's true mistress, the one whose name the fellowship will invoke as often as Arthur's own when a knight rides out to prove himself worthy of a place at her table.
stops.quote: never to do outrageousity nor murder, and always to flee treason... and always to do ladies, damosels, and gentlewomen succour, upon pain of death
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book III, ch. 15 (the Pentecostal Oath)

stops.name: Caerleon, the queen crowned apart
stops.campa: At Whitsuntide the City of the Legions fills for the crown-wearing, and Geoffrey's Britain keeps a rite the later romances forget. The queen is crowned apart. Her own archbishops and bishops conduct her, not to Arthur's church but to the Temple of Virgins, and four queens walk before her bearing four white doves as ancient custom requires, a retinue of women following after in open joy. Two courts sit that day, two churches, two crowns, and the feast is not complete until both are kept. Here Guinevere is no ornament of the king's table but a sovereignty running beside his.
stops.quote: On another part was the queen, dressed out in her richest ornaments, conducted by the archbishops and bishops to the Temple of Virgins; the four queens also of the kings last mentioned, bearing before her four white doves according to ancient custom; and after her there followed a retinue of women, making all imaginable demonstrations of joy.
stops.quote_source: Geoffrey of Monmouth, Historia Regum Britanniae, Book IX, ch. 13, trans. Aaron Thompson

stops.name: Camelot, Lancelot's coming
stops.campa: Out of the lake-country of Gaul rides Lancelot du Lac, and from the day Arthur knights him he is bound first to the king and, by the custom of the age's greatest romance, no less to the queen he serves as her own knight. Guinevere receives his courtesy as her due and gives him, in turn, the favor that makes him unmatched in every tournament he enters for her sake. The court does not yet call it anything but chivalry: a queen's champion riding out in her colors, proving, joust after joust, that no shield in Christendom stands higher than hers.

stops.name: Glastonbury, the marshes of the Summer Country
stops.campa: Melwas, king of the Summer Country, carries off Guinevere and brings her behind the reed-beds and river-braid of his stronghold at the Glass Town, where causeways vanish into marsh and no army can safely follow. Arthur searches a whole year before he hears she is there, then rouses the armies of Cornubia and Dibneria and lays siege to a place ringed by water on every side. The abduction is no rumor here, no allegory: Caradoc of Llancarfan sets it down as history, the earliest hand to write that a king's wife was taken and a king marched to get her back.
stops.quote: It was besieged by the tyrant Arthur with a countless multitude on account of his wife Gwenhwyfar, whom the aforesaid wicked king had violated and carried off, and brought there for protection
stops.quote_source: Caradoc of Llancarfan, Vita Gildae (Life of St Gildas), section 10, trans. Hugh Williams (1899)

stops.name: Glastonbury Abbey, the peace of Gildas
stops.campa: Before the marsh can be forced, the abbot of Glastonbury steps into the space between the contending armies with Gildas the Wise and his clergy beside him, unarmed, and in a peaceable manner advises Melwas, his own king, to restore the ravished lady. Melwas yields the queen; the two kings, reconciled, give the abbot many domains in thanks and promise before the brothers never to violate so sacred a place again. Guinevere returns to her husband unharmed by the telling, restored in peace and good will rather than by the sword, and Glastonbury keeps, from that day forward, a claim on her story that will not let go of it.
stops.quote: Accordingly, she who was to be restored, was restored in peace and good will.
stops.quote_source: Caradoc of Llancarfan, Vita Gildae, section 11, trans. Hugh Williams (1899)

stops.name: Camelot, the queen's champion
stops.campa: Years deepen what began as courtesy. Lancelot rides for no other favor, wears no color but hers into the lists, and returns each time to lay the day's honor at her feet, quietly, the way a vassal lays it before his lord. The court reads it as pageantry, the highest knight paying the highest lady her due, and for a long while pageantry is all it needs to be. Only Agravain and Mordred, watching too closely, begin to name in the hall's dim corners what everyone else has agreed, for the fellowship's sake, not to see.

stops.name: Westminster, the poisoned apple
stops.campa: Guinevere makes a private dinner for four-and-twenty knights of the Table and sets out fruit, because Gawain loves apples and pears and everyone who feasts him knows it. Sir Pinel le Savage, who means to avenge Lamorak on Gawain, poisons one; Sir Patrise of Ireland takes it, swells till he bursts, and falls dead among them. Because the queen made the feast, the suspicion is hers. Mador de la Porte appeals her of treason and not one knight will stand for her; Bors consents only on condition; Lancelot comes at the hour's end and overthrows Mador. It is the first time she is condemned to the fire.
stops.quote: considering Queen Guenever made the feast and dinner, they all had suspicion unto her
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XVIII, ch. 3

stops.name: Astolat, the red sleeve and the barge
stops.campa: At Astolat, which Malory names for Guildford, Lancelot lodges with Sir Bernard and, to ride the Winchester jousts unknown, does the one thing he has never done for any woman: he wears another's token, the red sleeve of Elaine le Blank. The queen hears of it and is past reason with him, and Bors pleads that he bore it only so that his own blood should not know him. Elaine, refused, dies of it, and comes down the river to Westminster in a barge with a letter still in her hand. Guinevere reads it, and blames him not for the love but for the coldness.
stops.quote: Ye might have shewed her some bounty and gentleness that might have preserved her life.
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XVIII, ch. 20

stops.name: Westminster, the Maying and the Knight of the Cart
stops.campa: In the month of May the queen gives warning that she will ride a-Maying into the woods and fields beside Westminster, and takes ten knights of the Table with her, all clothed in green, silk or cloth, each with a lady behind him, and no armour in the company. Sir Meliagrance has watched for exactly this season and this absence: he falls on the party with twenty men of arms and a hundred archers. Her knights fight until they are cut to pieces, and she surrenders herself to save their lives, on the one condition that they stay beside her. Lancelot comes after her in a woodcutter's cart.
stops.quote: the month of May was come, when every lusty heart beginneth to blossom, and to bring forth fruit; for like as herbs and trees bring forth fruit and flourish in May, in like wise every lusty heart that is in any manner a lover, springeth and flourisheth in lusty deeds
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XVIII, ch. 25 (the May prologue to the Knight of the Cart)

stops.name: Carlisle, accused and condemned to the fire
stops.campa: Agravain and Mordred hide twelve knights in a chamber of the Castle of Carlisle and take the queen and Lancelot together, and though he cuts his way out through the chamber door, Guinevere is taken. Arthur, bound by the law he himself upholds, cannot save her by his own hand: treason found in the deed admits no remedy but death, and the sentence the court itself swore to keep is the fire. She is led forth without the city and despoiled into her smock, to be burned before the fellowship whose oath she has broken, the same fellowship that once knelt to swear mercy in her name.
stops.quote: then the queen was led forth without Carlisle, and there she was despoiled into her smock
stops.quote_source: Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XX, ch. 8
